title: K-P-R
hook: kaparah, Yom Kippur: to cover over, to wipe clean

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-T-A: chet, the slinger's stone that flies wide, the free throw off the rim. Your line was sin is missing the mark. What adjustment did you make? Today, what comes after the miss. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

"Make thee an ark of gopher wood." Noah gets his instructions in Genesis: the wood, the rooms, the measurements. And one more step, easy to skip past. Before the rain, before the animals, the whole boat has to be sealed. Every seam, every gap between boards, smeared over with thick, dark pitch, inside and out, so the water can't get in. It's sticky, unglamorous work. But without it, the ark is a very large box that sinks. Keep that pot of pitch in view. Its Hebrew name shares three letters with a holy day on the Jewish calendar. Kaf, fey, resh: K-P-R.
screen: `MAKE THEE AN ARK.` → `SEAL EVERY SEAM WITH PITCH.` → `K-P-R: COVER.`

segments.voice: Turn K-P-R four ways. First, the pitch. Genesis says Noah "shalt pitch it within and without with pitch." Both words, to pitch and the pitch, come from this root: kofer, a coating that covers. Second, the cover. When Moses is told how to build the ark of the covenant, the box that holds the tablets, it gets a lid of pure gold called the kapporet, the ark-cover. On it, the text says, God will meet with Moses. A covering, again, and a holy one. Third, the day. Yom Kippur, the day of kippurim, of atonements. Leviticus describes it this way: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." Atonement there is from the same root. So hear both pictures in it: covering over, like pitch on a seam, and wiping clean, like a cleansed slate. Fourth, the catch. The Mishnah, near the end of tractate Yoma, adds a line about preparing for the day. For wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between one person and another, Yom Kippur does not atone until the wrongdoer makes peace with the person they hurt. The day can't do that part for you. So before the fast, some people call each other. Some knock on doors. They say, I'm sorry for what I said in the spring. So atonement covers. But like Noah's pitch, it doesn't spread itself. Someone has to pick up the brush and work it into the seam, one gap at a time, until the water can't get through.
screen: `KOFER: PITCH, INSIDE AND OUT.` · `KAPPORET: THE GOLDEN ARK-COVER.` · `YOM KIPPUR: COVERED, CLEANSED.` · `BETWEEN PEOPLE: GO TO THEM FIRST.` · then, large: `כַּפָּרָה`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cover one wrong with good. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small wrong you did that still has a gap in it. A word that stung, a call you didn't return, a favor you let drop. Picture the person. Now picture the brush and the pitch: one good thing you could do that would cover that seam. An apology, plain and specific. A call. The favor, done late. Choose it, and see yourself doing it. If you pray, you can bring that person into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
K-P-R. Kaf, fey, resh: kofer, the pitch on Noah's ark; kapporet, the ark-cover; kaparah, atonement, as in Yom Kippur. To cover over, to wipe clean. Today's word.
Your line: atonement covers. Today, do the good thing you chose, for the person you wronged, and let it be specific enough that they know what it's for. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally seek out people they may have wronged to ask forgiveness, following the Mishnah's teaching that the day atones for wrongs between people only once the wronged person has been appeased; the day itself is kept with fasting and prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: atonement means paying a penalty.
what it means: the root of kaparah means to cover over and to wipe clean.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Yoma 8:9: between people, the day atones only after the wrongdoer appeases the one wronged.

notes: Editor: Yoma 8:9 placed 'near the end' of the tractate; 'people call each other' softened to 'some people'; cut the stock line 'Nobody writes songs about it'; varied the 'Hold onto that' and 'Put it together' phrasing used on nearby days.
Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 6:14 and Leviticus 16:30 as quoted.
Exodus 25:17-22 paraphrased (kapporet of pure gold; God will meet Moses there). JPS 1917 renders kapporet 'ark-cover'; confirm.
Mishnah Yoma 8:9 paraphrased; 'at the end of tractate Yoma' assumes 8:9 is near the close of the tractate. Confirm.
'Kofer' as pitch and 'kaparah' as covering follow the outline's 'to cover over, to wipe clean'; the etymological link is debated among scholars (covering vs. wiping).
